mcqs.question: Both brute-force enumeration and backtracking walk the same decision tree over the same choices. What actually distinguishes backtracking from brute force?
options: Backtracking uses recursion while brute force must be iterative
Backtracking always finds fewer valid solutions than brute force
Backtracking checks validity as early as possible and stops descending into dead branches, instead of checking only at complete leaves
Backtracking never revisits a node, while brute force can visit the same node twice
mcqs.explanation: The tree and the final set of valid solutions are identical either way — the only difference is when invalidity is detected. Backtracking prunes a dead branch the moment it's known to be dead, so it never descends into the subtree beneath it, while brute force builds full candidates before filtering. Both can be implemented recursively or iteratively, and neither revisits nodes.

mcqs.question: In the generic backtracking skeleton, why does the `is_valid` check run before `choose(state, candidate)` rather than after?
options: So invalid candidates are skipped without ever being added to the state, avoiding an unnecessary choose/unexplore pair
Because Python requires all validation to happen before any function call
It doesn't matter — checking after choosing produces identical performance
So that recursion depth is tracked correctly
mcqs.explanation: Checking before choosing means a doomed candidate never touches the state at all — no mutation, no recursive call, no undo needed. Checking after choosing would still be correct if paired with an undo, but it does strictly more work per rejected candidate, so placement is a real performance choice, not a cosmetic one, and has nothing to do with depth tracking.

mcqs.question: A backtracking function pushes each choice onto a shared `path` list but never pops it after the recursive call returns. What's the observable symptom?
options: The program raises a RecursionError immediately
It runs correctly but takes longer than expected
The very first solution found is already wrong, but later ones are correct
The first solution found is correct, but every solution after it is corrupted by leftover choices from earlier branches
mcqs.explanation: The first branch explored never has a sibling's leftovers in the state, so it comes out right — the corruption only appears starting with the second branch, once a prior choice that should have been undone is still sitting in `path`. This is what makes the bug easy to miss in a quick manual check: it doesn't crash and the first result looks fine.

mcqs.question: For N-Queens at N = 8, pruning on column and diagonal conflicts explores only a few thousand partial boards instead of brute force's ~16.7 million full placements. What does pruning change about the answer set?
options: It finds a subset of the valid solutions, trading completeness for speed
It changes which placements count as valid
Nothing about the answer set — pruning only changes how much dead search is skipped along the way
It requires re-deriving the problem's constraints from scratch
mcqs.explanation: Pruning is purely an efficiency mechanism: it detects the same invalid states brute force would eventually discard, just earlier, before wasting work building out the rest of that branch. The final set of valid boards is identical either way — pruning doesn't redefine validity or sacrifice completeness.

mcqs.question: Why does pruning a branch near the root of the search tree save more work than pruning an equivalent branch near a leaf?
options: Root-level pruning eliminates an entire subtree of roughly b^(remaining depth) nodes, while leaf-level pruning only removes a handful of nodes
Root-level checks are cheaper to compute than leaf-level checks
It doesn't — pruning saves the same fixed amount of work regardless of where it happens
Leaf-level pruning is actually more valuable because it catches errors closer to the final answer
mcqs.explanation: Cutting a branch at depth k removes everything that would have branched out from it — roughly b raised to the remaining depth — so an early cut removes an exponentially larger chunk of the tree than a late one. This is about how much of the tree is skipped, not about the cost of the check itself or where errors are 'caught.'

mcqs.question: A backtracking N-Queens solution builds a full 8-row board and only then checks whether it's a valid arrangement. It's correct but times out on larger N. What's the most likely fix?
options: Switch from recursion to an iterative implementation
Increase the recursion depth limit
Move the validity check to run after each individual queen is placed, not only once the board is complete
Reduce the number of columns considered at each row
mcqs.explanation: Checking only at a complete board means every invalid partial placement still gets built out to full depth before being discarded — the fix is to validate each placement immediately so dead branches are cut as early as possible. This is a pruning-placement issue, not a recursion-vs-iteration or depth-limit issue, and columns can't be arbitrarily dropped without changing correctness.
